core: Art as a historically and culturally situated category rather than a universal checklist
The difference between observation, interpretation, and evaluative judgment
How material, maker, setting, use, audience, and reception shape an account of a work
Why beauty, originality, skill, and institutional recognition may matter without being universal requirements

Close looking as a basis for a cautious interpretation

claims.claim: There is no single simple definition that reliably separates every work called art from every artifact; questions about the category are central to art history itself.
Beauty and originality have each been influential ways of thinking about art, but neither is a universal attribute of the works studied in art history.

Getty's Art & Architecture Thesaurus uses 'works of art' for works in any medium, including performance art, showing that professional vocabularies can classify a broad range of practices without settling every philosophical boundary.

UNESCO's 2005 Convention describes cultural expressions as resulting from the creativity of individuals, groups, and societies and having cultural content; it treats cultural diversity as expressed through varied artistic creation, production, dissemination, distribution, and enjoyment.
A responsible introductory interpretation separates what can be observed in or documented about a work from inferences about meaning, then identifies the evidence and limits of the inference.

A work's material, process, maker or community, setting, intended or recorded use, audience, and later reception can provide relevant context; no one factor automatically determines whether something is art or what it means.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether art should be defined by beauty, skilled making, originality, visual impact, institutional recognition, or another single property.
positions: Historical accounts show beauty and originality have been influential criteria in particular settings.
The works and cultural expressions studied by art history include practices for which those criteria are insufficient or misleading.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson does not impose a universal definition. It treats 'art' as a category whose use requires description, context, and a stated reason for the classification, while recognizing that reasonable interpretations can remain contested.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft called the topic a generic foundational concept but supplied no account of art, art history, cultural context, or interpretive limits.
Its vocabulary definition for the topic was circular, its college version was generic study-skills prose, and its three quick-check items had only three options.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced template language with a source-verified explanation of art as a contested and context-sensitive category.
Added distinctions among observation, interpretation, and evaluation so that subjective response is neither dismissed nor confused with evidence.
Added culturally sensitive framing that does not assume a Western fine-art model, a market value, or an individual artist is the only relevant context.
Rebuilt assessment as five four-option questions spanning recall, understanding, application, and analysis.

sourceRecords.notes: Read as the principal Tier B introductory source. sourceRecords.title: Convention on the Protection and Promotion of the Diversity of Cultural Expressions (2005)
sourceRecords.notes: Read to verify its definitions of cultural diversity, cultural content, and cultural expressions and its principle of equal dignity and respect for cultures. The lesson uses this only for a broad cultural-expression framework and does not give legal or policy advice.
